Well I was, I, you know I would be in and then I would drop out and then I would get back in and drop out. Well I've been in this stretch, this stretch I've been in since 19, I think since 1960. Oh, oh maybe before that. I don't think I dropped out. I think I transferred over from when they integrated it too. So maybe I've been in now, this time. No I just straightened up. So it got to be in the late 60s, maybe about 67, maybe before then. I've been in since then. But before that I was in and out. See because when we had the black local, you know, first of all they said I owed them a whole lot of tax, but I paid them. But they also had two set of books. There was the secretary who, you know, you were going there and paying, she'd mark it up in this book and then put it in that book. Well they never did prosecute nobody, but a lot of money went another way. It was the black, 496. You see, I know personally I had bought union cards. See like if I had to go to like Pritchett, Alabama, because we would all go that way. If I go to Florida, you had to have a union card. I'd go there and get a lady ten dollars and get me a union card, pay it up. But I just had to remember that Monday morning I had to come back to the hall and tear it up in front of her.
So the unions were pretty strict, wherever you played, they would check?

Yeah, they would check, you know. And more hassle, you know, than anything. That right to work wasn't so much enforced then like it is now. Because the union don't even bother you no more. They leave it up to you to take care. See like last Friday night I played at the Royal Lawley bourbon all the time. And I paid them yesterday. They don't bother me no more because I'm going to pay them, but I'm going to cheat them too first year every time I get. And I guess they know that. Because the union, our union really does nothing for nobody. Now, I'm going to say this. See, I was told that a quarter of a million dollars was the word goes through the union every year. Now, I heard, I got this from one guy, I won't call his name, but anyway, he got me to be on his, to run on his ticket on a wage committee. And so I went to a few meetings on St. Charles Avenue when a good Jewish friend of mine, I ain't going to call no name. But anyway, I went to some meetings and I learned some things about the union, about money. It's about a quarter of a million dollars that go through the union. And he wanted to know why he didn't get some of that work. Now, you know what happened? He's on the board now. And he go there, I know he'd look at me and say nothing, but he know I know. But I don't shake, you know. I have mentioned it. I mentioned it not too long ago about this money that, see, being a union, I know people call me for work. Right. Okay, I'm just a band leader. I know people from all over the world call a musician union. You know, just simple as that. Well, they're supposed to. That's what I'm telling you. If you ask for a piano player, they're supposed to just, I think, you know, there's a list of a hundred people. But you know better than that. Right. Yeah. Now, okay, this is what this guy was talking about, and this is really what it is. Now, when I mention that, you know what he said? Mr. Dillon, are you referring to my office? I want to bring you before the board for that. I said, well, you got to bring me before the board, bring me before the board. Yeah. But you know what? They brought me before the board. Yeah. Ain't going to bring me. But you know, now, you know, they talk to me, and I go down there, and they're talking about how bad business is right now. Business is bad. They ain't getting no money. Ain't no money coming in, because there ain't too many people working. They got people working who are non-union. And every so often, I tell them, but I say, all these people, I say, all these non-union musicians, that's what you ought to try to do something about. And they don't say anything about that. Mr. Weinstein is the best man. Oh, that's a good man. That's a good man. He's wonderful. He's the best. You know, I know he's the president of all over. You know, he's also the vice president of the International.
Yeah.

But he is basically a good man. And you can go there and get any information you want. But I do know one thing. He's just in part of the thing. He's part of the clique. And there ain't nothing much he can do. But what he did for Professor Longhair, this is when I really found out that he's a good man. You see, Professor Longhair was taken. The Fess was taken. And when Mr. Weinstein found out about it, and he took over Fess's business, that's why whatever Professor Longhair had right now today is because of Mr. Weinstein. Nobody else but him. Because he took over. And he tell me, you know what he tell me? He said, tell me, man, let me tell you something. He said, man, y'all go down and sign all them papers and have all them crooks taking all your money and things. He said, look, when you get a piece of paper, tell me what you do. He said, if you have something and you don't quite understand, he said, look, just find time to come on down here. He said, let me look over for you. And this is what, and he emphasized it all the time, but I still don't do it. But basically a good man, that's all.
What about your dealings with 496 over the years? What did you do about it?

496, well, they had me before the boat every other week. Well, for failing to file a contract. I didn't do this yet. You know, and I thought there was a bunch of dogs. In fact, the union as a whole, I think, you know, people, a lot of people get on me when I say this because there are people who are strictly unionized. I'm not unionized. I feel like we can get, we can make it without the union because, because what the union do for them? I think the unions have outlived their usefulness. I think it's, I think that, you can forget about the union, not because everybody know about how much money they deserve to make, and just as a whole. And I think people know just about what they're supposed to pay. And I don't need no man to buy to come in and say so and so and so is the case, and now you bring me some of your money, because that's all the union does. Yeah.
Well, the union, I heard they were notorious years ago. They would sit on your session. Mm-hm.
I heard they were notorious years ago, they would sit on each session.

Oh, oh, they had a delegate, Mr. Green. Mr. Green was a delegate. He would come around there and, you know, you would record. He would come there, but if people didn't look right, he would stop it. Stop the recording session. But no, he wasn't.

segments.title: Session opening, third interview
segments.summary: Opening chatter, then Tad Jones announces the third session, June 20, 1986, at Ridgley's River Ridge house, resuming at In the Same Old Way.

segments.title: How Eddie Bo's ballad became In the Same Old Way
segments.summary: Ridgley changed Eddie Bo's slow ballad to an up tempo; the WYLD program director told him to take it to Larry McKinley. Only other easy radio break was Papa Stopper and When I Meet My Girl.

segments.title: Ila show for Larry McKinley pays $10
segments.summary: Ridgley, Earl King and Ernie Cato packed the ILA show; he brought ten pieces for $150 and McKinley gave him $10.

segments.title: Three Times and Chuck Cornish's songs on Rick
segments.summary: Ridgley recalls the Rick record Three Times and its flip, written by Chuck Cornish, and how songs came from outside writers while Eddie Bo was the main writer.

segments.title: A Girl from Cucamonga and the Double Whammy dispute
segments.summary: Who decided what was recorded; Girl from Cucamonga as an Oop-Oop-A-Doo takeoff, and Freddie King's chart hit with Double Whammy that Ridgley plans to pursue through an attorney.

segments.title: Live While You Can for Mr. Walker's Dew Drop label
segments.summary: Tad brings out other labels; Ridgley describes recording Live While You Can in Jackson with Wardell's arrangement, and refusing Mr. Walker a co-writer credit.

segments.title: Leaving Rick and Joe Ruffino
segments.summary: Ridgley demanded a release from Ruffino, leaving Johnny Adams; he left around Ruffino's 1962 death and hopes to regain his Rick songs after 27 years.

segments.title: All My Love Belongs to You and I Want Some Money on One Stop
segments.summary: Joe Assunto's One Stop record; Eddie Bo's funky I Want Some Money was changed by Wardell's arrangement; London did not promote it, recorded at Cosmo.

segments.title: Blue Jay: Call on My Baby with brother Sammy and Johnny Adams
segments.summary: Eddie Bo set up the Groovy Gus record; Ridgley's brother Sammy could not sing harmony so Johnny Adams sang the other part.

segments.title: Payola and the disc jockey who could break a record
segments.summary: Disc jockeys and program directors expected money; Ridgley describes a DJ who could break records and the flip side Pretty Little Mama.

segments.title: Bob Robin's River City Records and the Baton Rouge session
segments.summary: Ridgley recalls River City sides recorded in Baton Rouge with Bob Robin, a guitarist's playing, and unreleased tracks and a good-selling record.

segments.title: I'm Not the Same Person and the Cinderella label
segments.summary: The B side of In the Same Old Way, then Cinderella, the Smith record shop label on St. Charles with Eddie Bo arranging.

segments.title: Cosmo session arranged by Edward Frank
segments.summary: A Cosmo single Ridgley wrote, arranged by Edward Frank, who also botched the first Live While You Can; Skip Godwin engineered.

segments.title: International City record in Mississippi with Bob Robin
segments.summary: Ridgley wrote lyrics to pre-taped tracks at Huey Meaux's Mississippi studio, with white musicians and a Motown feel; My Love Gets Stronger.

segments.title: Spreading Life and remixing Live While You Can
segments.summary: Eddie Bo talked Ridgley into funding a label for a tune already cut; Ridgley remixed the Live While You Can master from Mrs. Walker's tape with Allen Toussaint's help.

segments.title: Tudor Square and half the publishing on Sometime You Get It
segments.summary: Ridgley recorded for Sansu, the station dropped it for lack of money, and Marshall agreed to give half the publishing so Ridgley could release it on Tudor Square.

segments.title: Help Me, the Japanese reissue and Marshall Sehorn's check
segments.summary: Ridgley covered a Bill Anderson country song; Marshall Sehorn sold the soul sides to a Japanese label, paying Ridgley $200 by a bounced check; Shack Up and the New Orleans symphony strings.

segments.title: Sound of New Orleans and Gary Edwards: no pay
segments.summary: Saints-themed songs by Janice Medlow recorded for Gary Edwards; Ridgley never got paid though musicians and Wardell were.

segments.title: Ruffino's two sets of books and how many records Ridgley made
segments.summary: Ruffino paid small sums, no royalty statements and kept two sets of books; records kept Ridgley's name alive, perhaps in the 50s counted.

segments.title: The Untouchables and what a good band needs
segments.summary: Ridgley praises the original Untouchables who could read, and complains about his current band, stressing the drummer and bass.

segments.title: Young black musicians cannot play the blues
segments.summary: Ridgley laments that young New Orleans black musicians in 1986 don't know blues or read, so he hires white players.

segments.title: What a drummer should do: two hands, sock cymbal, back beat
segments.summary: Ridgley criticizes his present mechanical drummer and says a drummer needs two good hands, the 6/8 rhythm and the back beat.

segments.title: Earl Palmer and musicians who could play everything
segments.summary: Nobody better than Earl Palmer; years ago players could play everything, today they are in categories and some cannot read.

segments.title: The Dixieland parade roots of New Orleans R&B drumming
segments.summary: Ridgley thinks the drumming, from the Dixieland parade syncopation and two-beat bass and drum, makes the music distinct.

segments.title: What rock and roll meant, and the white musicians now
segments.summary: To Ridgley rock and roll meant white audiences; once black bands played white dances, now white musicians back black singers; Bobby Cure and shared rhythm.

segments.title: Ridgley as a rock and roll artist
segments.summary: He was a rock and roll artist, played white colleges across the region, and had a sing-along act with his band.

segments.title: Traveling by station wagon with the band
segments.summary: Seven men and instruments in one 1957 station wagon, with Justin Adams's tall tales and band camaraderie.

segments.title: Finding black neighborhoods, road trips and $500 in Shreveport
segments.summary: Where they stayed on the road, mostly overnight gigs, and Abbe Goldberg booking $500 dates in Shreveport after When I Meet My Girl.

segments.title: Joining the union and the black local 496's books
segments.summary: Ridgley's in-and-out union membership since 1949, bought cards, double books at the black local.

segments.title: Union checks, money and the board
segments.summary: Ridgley on right to work, a quarter million dollars through the union, and being threatened with the board.

segments.title: Mr. Weinstein and Professor Longhair
segments.summary: Weinstein is a good man in the clique who took over Professor Longhair's business.

segments.title: Ridgley's view of the union and recording-session delegates
segments.summary: He thinks unions have outlived usefulness; Tad recalls delegates sitting in on sessions, and Mr. Green stopping recordings.
